common_name: AU Golden Dragon Kiwi (Auburn University Low-Chill Golden Kiwifruit)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines after frost danger passes on a heavy-gauge overhead arbor or T-bar trellis; this is a dioecious golden kiwi selection, so a male Actinidia chinensis pollenizer must be planted within about 30 feet for fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, training the vigorous vine onto a permanent overhead arbor or T-bar trellis from the start. AU Golden Dragon was an earlier golden-kiwi release from Auburn University's low-chill breeding program, predating and paving the way for the later AU Golden Sunshine selection, which ripens roughly three weeks after it; both were bred specifically to fruit reliably under the mild, low-chill winters of the Deep South rather than requiring the colder winters standard green-fleshed 'Hayward' kiwi needs. Fruit is smooth-skinned with sweet, aromatic golden flesh and high sugar content, best harvested firm and ripened at room temperature. Because gold-fleshed Actinidia chinensis types are more prone to bacterial canker (Psa) than green-fleshed A. deliciosa, avoid overhead irrigation, prune annually to keep the canopy open, and disinfect pruning tools between plants.
sources: Auburn University College of Agriculture — kiwifruit research
Alabama Cooperative Extension System — small fruit variety notes

common_name: Excalibur Pecan (University of Georgia Scab-Resistant Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained bottomland-type soil; Excalibur is a Type II pollen shedder and needs a Type I cultivar such as Elliott or Desirable nearby for a full nut set.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun, siting a compatible Type I pollinator within range since pecans are wind-pollinated and set poorly from a single cultivar. Excalibur was released from the University of Georgia pecan breeding program at Tifton, selected primarily for its strong resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that causes the most consistent yield losses for home and commercial growers across the humid Gulf South, letting it produce a reliable crop with far less fungicide input than older scab-susceptible standards. Nuts are large with good kernel quality and a bright, attractive shell. Supplement with an annual zinc sulfate foliar spray, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders, and harvest once the shucks split open in October and November.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Pecan variety trials, Tifton
American Pecan Council — recommended cultivar notes

common_name: AU Gobbler I Chestnut (Auburn University Wildlife Food-Plot Chinese Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU Gobbler I is the earlier of Auburn's two Gobbler-series chestnuts and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Gobbler I was the original release in Auburn University's Gobbler line of Chinese chestnut selections, bred under the same heat-, humidity-, and disease-pressure conditions of the Deep South as the university's other chestnut releases and later followed by the extended-drop AU Gobbler II. It was selected for dependable annual nut drop timed to coincide with fall wildlife food-plot season, making it a favorite of hunters and land managers as well as home orchardists who want a blight-resistant, low-input nut tree. Space trees widely for a broad mature canopy and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a good crop.
sources: Auburn University College of Agriculture — Chestnut Breeding Program
wildlife food plot nursery variety notes

common_name: Crimson Plum (Auburn University Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for the Gulf South)

planting.note: Set out bare-root or container trees in late winter while dormant, in full sun with sharply drained soil to avoid Prunus root rot problems; Crimson needs roughly 650 hours of winter chilling, so it performs most reliably in zone 8 and cooler zone 9 pockets of the Gulf South.

directions: Crimson was released by the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station as one of the earlier selections in its Japanese-American 'Au' plum breeding line, later giving rise to the darker-fruited sport AU-Rubrum. Trees are self-fruitful but set noticeably heavier crops when a second Japanese or Japanese-American plum, such as Methley or another Au-series variety, is planted within pollinating range. Fruit ripens in late spring to early summer with dark red skin and sweet, juicy red flesh well suited to fresh eating and preserves. Like the rest of the Au series, it was bred specifically for resistance to bacterial canker, bacterial leaf spot, and black knot, giving it a real advantage over older plum varieties under the humid, disease-prone growing conditions of the Southeast.

common_name: Umran Indian Jujube (Large-Fruited Ber for South Texas and the Gulf Coast)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, lean to average, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Umran is more heat- and drought-tolerant than Chinese jujube but far less cold-hardy, so it is best suited to zone 9-10 South Texas, the Rio Grande Valley, and the mildest parts of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Umran is one of the most widely grown named selections of Indian jujube (ber), prized in its native South Asia for producing unusually large, round to oval fruit that ripens from green to a mottled yellow-brown and is eaten fresh while still crisp and apple-like, well before it wrinkles into a date-like dried stage. Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil, since Umran resents wet feet and performs best with infrequent, deep watering once established. The tree bears young and heavily, often within two to three years of planting, and tolerates heat, drought, and poor soils far better than most temperate fruit trees, making it a productive dual-season option for the hottest, driest microclimates of zone 9-10 Gulf Coast gardens. Thin overcrowded fruit clusters in years of heavy set to improve individual fruit size, and protect young trees from any frost since Umran has little cold tolerance compared to Chinese jujube (Ziziphus jujuba).
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — subtropical fruit variety notes
UF IFAS Extension — minor tropical fruit publications

common_name: Crimson Mayhaw (Improved Western Mayhaw for Gulf South Jelly Production)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; Crimson is one of several named improved mayhaw selections and sets a heavier crop with a second mayhaw cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, taking advantage of mayhaw's unusual tolerance for the poorly drained, low-lying bottomland where most other fruit trees decline. Crimson is a named western mayhaw selection grown alongside cultivars such as Texas Star and Super Berry by Gulf South orchardists seeking improved, more consistent fruit production than wild-collected mayhaw offers, bearing clusters of small, tart, aromatic red berries that ripen in May. As with all mayhaw selections, fruit is gathered from the ground or shaken onto tarps and processed quickly into the region's traditional mayhaw jelly, since the berries are too tart and dry for fresh eating. Plant a second, genetically distinct mayhaw cultivar within range for the best cross-pollination and yield, and expect three to five years to first bearing with production increasing steadily over the following decade.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — native fruit variety notes

common_name: Super Berry Mayhaw (Large-Fruited Western Mayhaw Selection)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; Super Berry is grown for its above-average fruit size and sets a heavier crop with a second mayhaw cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a wetland-adapted native tree that thrives on low, poorly drained ground unsuitable for most conventional fruit trees. Super Berry is a named western mayhaw selection valued by Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi growers for producing noticeably larger fruit than wild-collected trees or many older seedling selections, packed into heavy clusters of bright red, tart, aromatic berries that ripen in May. The larger fruit size speeds hand harvest for home jelly-making, one of the enduring food traditions of the Gulf South. Plant alongside a second mayhaw cultivar, such as Texas Star or Crimson, for the best cross-pollination and yield, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years, becoming increasingly productive as it matures over the following decade.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — native fruit variety notes
